# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

Ask ten developers how they wire an AI assistant to their tools and you will get ten different answers: a bespoke REST client here, a GraphQL wrapper there, a pile of shell scripts nobody dares to touch. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, replaces that zoo with a single, open standard.

MCP defines one simple contract: a server exposes tools, resources and prompts; a client — an AI assistant, an IDE, a CMS — discovers them and calls them. No more per-integration glue code. Write the server once and every MCP-capable client can use it.

What makes it awesome is not the protocol itself but what it unlocks. Tools become composable. Your editor, your terminal and your deployment pipeline can share the same capabilities, because they all speak the same language.

" Post 1 image block: image = network-lines-dots, caption "Every node connected: MCP turns isolated tools into a network. Photo by Conny Schneider on Unsplash." Post 1 rich text block 2: "

On this very site, the Umbraco MCP server models the schema, imports the media and publishes the pages — all through the same protocol this post is praising. Document types, data types, templates, domains: created, verified and wired together without a single hand-written migration file.

The practical win is speed with safety. Because every operation goes through Umbraco's own management API, validation still runs, uSync still exports, and the content tree stays the single source of truth. MCP does not bypass the CMS; it finally gives the CMS a front door that assistants can walk through.

If you are building anything with AI in 2026, bet on MCP. The ecosystem is growing daily, and the protocol is simple enough to implement in an afternoon.

" Post 1 quote block: quote "MCP is the USB-C of AI integrations: one port, every device, no more dongle drawer." attribution "The MCP Blog" Post 2 rich text block 1: "

Developers were the first to feel the magic of MCP, but content editors are quietly getting the biggest upgrade. When a CMS exposes itself over MCP, the backoffice stops being the only place where content work happens.

Imagine an editor sitting in their favourite writing tool, asking an assistant to draft a page, pick images from the media library, translate the copy and hit publish. The assistant calls the same MCP tools a human would click through — with the same permissions, the same validation and the same audit trail.

That is the superpower: editors keep their workflow, and the CMS keeps its rules. Nobody has to learn a new interface, because the interface they already use now understands the CMS.

" Post 2 image block: image = connected-structure, caption "One connected structure instead of a tangle of cables. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash." Post 2 rich text block 2: "

For teams, that means reviewable, repeatable, scriptable content operations. A new site? Model it once over MCP and every environment can be rebuilt from the same calls. A new post every week? The assistant does the typing; the editor does the judging.

Welcome to the MCP Blog — a small site built to show what happens when a CMS speaks the Model Context Protocol. Every page here was modeled, filled and published through MCP tools.

Start with the two posts below, or poke around the backoffice: the schema, the media library and the content tree tell the same story.

Ask ten developers how they wire an AI assistant to their tools and you will get ten different answers: a bespoke REST client here, a GraphQL wrapper there, a pile of shell scripts nobody dares to touch. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, replaces that zoo with a single, open standard.

MCP defines one simple contract: a server exposes tools, resources and prompts; a client — an AI assistant, an IDE, a CMS — discovers them and calls them. No more per-integration glue code. Write the server once and every MCP-capable client can use it.

What makes it awesome is not the protocol itself but what it unlocks. Tools become composable. Your editor, your terminal and your deployment pipeline can share the same capabilities, because they all speak the same language.

Developers were the first to feel the magic of MCP, but content editors are quietly getting the biggest upgrade. When a CMS exposes itself over MCP, the backoffice stops being the only place where content work happens.

Imagine an editor sitting in their favourite writing tool, asking an assistant to draft a page, pick images from the media library, translate the copy and hit publish. The assistant calls the same MCP tools a human would click through — with the same permissions, the same validation and the same audit trail.

That is the superpower: editors keep their workflow, and the CMS keeps its rules. Nobody has to learn a new interface, because the interface they already use now understands the CMS.

On this very site, the Umbraco MCP server models the schema, imports the media and publishes the pages — all through the same protocol this post is praising. Document types, data types, templates, domains: created, verified and wired together without a single hand-written migration file.

The practical win is speed with safety. Because every operation goes through Umbraco's own management API, validation still runs, uSync still exports, and the content tree stays the single source of truth. MCP does not bypass the CMS; it finally gives the CMS a front door that assistants can walk through.

If you are building anything with AI in 2026, bet on MCP. The ecosystem is growing daily, and the protocol is simple enough to implement in an afternoon.

The front page you are reading was assembled by an MCP-driven pipeline: a block grid of rich text, images and quotes, published under a domain, rendered by Razor views that follow Umbraco's own conventions. Every step — schema, media, content, publishing — happened through tools, not through hand-edited files.

For teams, that means reviewable, repeatable, scriptable content operations. A new site? Model it once over MCP and every environment can be rebuilt from the same calls. A new post every week? The assistant does the typing; the editor does the judging.

MCP is awesome because it turns the CMS from a walled garden into a well-lit workshop — and hands the editors the keys.

The site is still running. ## Report **What I built** — a working blog site in Umbraco.Bench, modeled and published entirely through the two MCP servers: - **Schema** (`umbraco`): three block element types (`richTextBlock`, `imageBlock`, `quoteBlock`) filed in the Blocks folder; a `Blog Block Grid` data type (12 columns, all three blocks, read back to confirm); `blogFrontPage` and `blogPost` page types in the Pages folder; templates wired via `update-document-type`; content tree `siteRoot → blogFrontPage → blogPost` with allowed children set accordingly. - **Media** (`umbraco`): a `Blog Images` folder with 4 Unsplash photos imported. - **Content** (`umbraco-editor`): a `Blog` front page under WWW and two published posts — *"Why MCP Is Awesome: One Protocol, Every Tool"* and *"Why MCP Is Awesome: Editors Get Superpowers Too"* — each with title, publish date, excerpt, listing image, and a 4-block body (rich text → image → rich text → quote). The front page has a title, intro, and a rich text block, and lists both posts (newest first) with link, title, date, excerpt, and cropped listing image. - **Domain**: `/` (en-US) assigned to the front page, so it answers at the site root. - **Rendering** (per AGENTS.md's pipeline): `Views/blogFrontPage.cshtml` and `Views/blogPost.cshtml` filled in place as full HTML pages rendering `@await Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync(Model, "body")`; three adapter-only partials in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/` mapping `BlockGridItem` to plain models in `Models/Blocks/`; three ViewComponents (`ViewComponents/`) with markup in `Views/Shared/Components//Default.cshtml`; Tailwind classes throughout, built via `npm run build` into `wwwroot/dist/site.css`. **How to view it** — Umbraco is running right now: open **https://localhost:44317/** (front page) and the two post URLs linked from it. To restart later: `cd Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco && dotnet run`. Backoffice: `/umbraco` (admin@example.com / 1234567890 — the scaffold default, change before anything real). **Verified with curl** — `/` and both posts return **200**; every block renders (8 paragraphs, figure+caption, blockquote per post; post cards on the front page); no literal `

` tags (rich text prints via `@Html.Raw`); no "Could not render component"; all images and the stylesheet return 200. `dotnet build` succeeds; uSync exported the schema. **Issues hit and fixed** (none outstanding): 1. `RichTextBlockModel` was ambiguous with Umbraco core's own `Umbraco.Cms.Core.Models.Blocks.RichTextBlockModel` in the adapters — fixed with a `using` alias in each adapter partial. 2. `publish-page` with `includeDescendants: true` returned "Publish cancelled" once; publishing the front page alone, then each post individually, worked (posts require their parent published first). **Not working / caveats**: nothing. One cosmetic note: the scaffold's `umb-block-grid` classes carry no CSS (per instructions I added none), so blocks stack full-width — each component view carries its own `my-8` spacing, which looks fine.
